extracted.intended_audience: law students, lawyers, scholars, and others researching U.S. administrative law and Supreme Court precedent
extracted.subtask_short: Auer deference and FLSA salary tests
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the Supreme Court's Auer v. Robbins holding on judicial deference to agencies' interpretations of their own regulations and explains related standards for FLSA salary-basis/exempt status and procedural requirements under the APA. Useful for understanding when courts will defer to agency interpretations and how the salary-basis test is applied to public-sector employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auer deference (agency interpretation of own regulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Auer deference gives agencies the highest level of deference in interpreting their own regulations; the agency's interpretation is controlling unless 'plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court gave deference to the Secretary of Labor's interpretation of the salary-basis test because the interpretation was 'based on a permissible construction of the statute.' Auer applies where the language of the regulation is ambiguous; it operates as a single-level standard of deference (distinct from Chevron's two-step framework).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference (agency interpretation of statutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron provides a two-step standard for judicial review of an agency's interpretation of its enabling statute: (1) whether Congress has directly spoken to the precise question; (2) if ambiguous, whether the agency's interpretation is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chevron addresses agency interpretation of statutes, while Auer addresses agency interpretation of the agency's own regulations. Auer was treated as expanding judicial deference in the regulatory-interpretation context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kisor v. Wilkie limitation on Auer
rubrics_metrics.description: Kisor v. Wilkie did not overturn Auer but set forth conditions where courts should use Auer deference, limiting its application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kisor focused on when courts may rely on Auer and imposed constraints on the extent of deference; the Wikipedia entry notes Kisor limited Auer's reach without wholly overruling it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary-basis test for FLSA exempt status
rubrics_metrics.description: For an employee to be exempt under the salary-basis test, the employee must earn a specified minimum amount on a salary basis and be paid a predetermined weekly payment that is not subject to reduction because of any variations in the 'quality or quantity of the work performed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department of Labor applied the salary-basis test since 1940; salary-basis status hinges on whether pay is 'subject to' reductions for quality/quantity variations. The Secretary's regulations define the contours of this test for determining exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: FLSA exemption categories (executive, administrative, professional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 13(a)(1) of the FLSA exempts 'bona fide executive, administrative, or professional' employees from overtime pay requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of exempt status requires satisfying both the salary-basis test and the duties test (i.e., the employee's job duties fit one of the exempt categories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of disciplinary pay deductions on salaried status
rubrics_metrics.description: A single or one-time disciplinary deduction does not necessarily defeat an employee's salaried (exempt) status; the mere possibility of deductions in a personnel manual is not enough if deductions are unlikely or not an anticipated form of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court upheld that a 'one-time incident' of deduction was a unique circumstance that did not destroy salaried status. Where a manual lists many possible penalties, 'no clear inference can be drawn as to the likelihood of a sanction' such that salaried status is defeated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood / anticipated practice standard for pay deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that salary is 'subject to' disciplinary deductions (and thus not salary-basis), there must be evidence that pay deductions are an anticipated or commonly applied form of discipline, not merely listed as a potential penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court emphasized that the presence of many possible rule violations and penalties in a manual does not demonstrate that pay deductions are an expected or routine sanction; the proper inquiry looks to the practical likelihood of deductions being applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency interpretations in legal briefs can receive deference
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency head's interpretation of its regulation set out in a legal brief may be entitled to deference and need not be disregarded as a post hoc rationalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court stated the Secretary's interpretation in a legal brief was 'in no way a post hoc rationalization' and therefore could be controlling under Auer, provided it was not plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA procedural requirement: exhaustion / petition to agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Administrative Procedure Act, parties should pursue the agency's regulatory appeals process (e.g., petition to the agency for rulemaking or other administrative remedies) rather than immediately seeking judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court noted that petitioners did not follow proper APA procedure and that the proper vehicle for challenging agency rules or seeking relief is to apply to the agency first; failure to do so can be a reason for courts to decline relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-sector policing of work rules does not automatically negate salaried status
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court rejected the argument that public-sector employees are categorically distinguished from private-sector employees for purposes of the salary-basis test because enforcing compliance with work rules is a necessary component of effective government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision affirms that the 1974 extension of the FLSA to cover public-sector employees means the same regulatory tests apply; the public-sector need for rule enforcement does not by itself render salary-basis regulations inapplicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of judicial review re: rulemaking vs. agency action
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims challenging that an agency acted arbitrarily or capriciously or failed to follow rulemaking procedures must be considered in the context of available administrative remedies; courts will not set aside agency action prior to any application for relief addressed to the agency itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court observed that the petitioners' claim was not that the regulation was substantively unlawful or lacked procedural prerequisites but rather that it was arbitrary not to conduct amendatory rulemaking; absent exhaustion of agency remedies, courts have limited basis to set aside agency action.
